procedural_history.originating_court: Presidency Magistrate's 4th Court at Girgaon, Bombay
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Revision Application No. 333 of 1964, dated August 25, 1964, dismissing a revision against the Magistrate's rejection of the accused-appellant's objection.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused-appellant filed a revision in the Bombay High Court against the Magistrate's rejection of his objection to the substitution of the complainant. The High Court dismissed the revision.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused-appellant, Ashwin Nanubhai Vyas, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the judgment and order of the Bombay High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the continued presence of the complainant, who is the 'person aggrieved' under Section 198 of the Criminal Procedure Code, is necessary for the continuation of a committal inquiry after cognizance has been taken on their complaint.

facts: A complaint was filed by an 'aggrieved person' (Kusum) for offences that, under Section 198 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), require such a complaint for a court to take cognizance.
After the Magistrate took cognizance of the complaint, the complainant died.
The complainant's mother applied to the court to continue the prosecution.
The accused argued that the proceedings must terminate (abate) because the 'aggrieved person' was no longer present, which they claimed was a continuous requirement for the court's jurisdiction.
law: Section 198 Cr.P.C. creates a bar on the court from taking cognizance of certain offences except upon a complaint made by a 'person aggrieved'.

Chapter XVIII of the Cr.P.C., which governs committal inquiries, does not contain any provision for the acquittal or discharge of the accused if the complainant fails to attend court after the proceedings have begun.
This is in contrast to the chapters on summons cases (s. 247) and warrant cases (s. 259), which explicitly provide for the acquittal or discharge of the accused upon the complainant's absence.
Section 495 Cr.P.C. empowers a court to authorize 'any person' to conduct a prosecution.
application: The Court interpreted Section 198 as a one-time requirement that must be met for the court to initially take cognizance of the case. Once a proper complaint is filed by the aggrieved person, the bar is removed, and the section's purpose is fulfilled ('it works itself out').

The Court reasoned that if the legislature had intended for the complainant's continued presence to be a requirement, it would have explicitly stated so in the Code, just as it did for summons and warrant cases.
The absence of a provision for discharge or acquittal in Chapter XVIII was seen as a 'deliberate departure', indicating that the inquiry should proceed even without the original complainant.
The Court rejected the argument that the proceedings abated upon the complainant's death, noting that the Code does not provide for the abatement of inquiries or trials in such a situation.

The Court held that the Magistrate had the power under Section 495 to allow the complainant's mother to continue the prosecution, clarifying that this was not an improper 'substitution' but an authorization for another person to conduct the case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument and held that the continued presence of the complainant is not necessary for the continuation of a committal inquiry after cognizance has been validly taken. The requirement of Section 198 is fulfilled once the initial complaint is filed by the aggrieved person, and the subsequent death or absence of that person does not terminate the proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the provisions for acquittal or discharge of an accused due to the complainant's absence in summons cases (Section 247) and warrant cases (Section 259) can be applied by analogy to a committal inquiry under Chapter XVIII of the Criminal Procedure Code.

facts: The case in question was not a trial of a summons case or a warrant case, but a committal inquiry being heard under Chapter XVIII of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The accused argued that the provisions for acquitting or discharging an accused due to the complainant's absence in summons cases (Section 247) and warrant cases (Section 259) should be applied by analogy to the committal inquiry.
law: Section 247, found in Chapter XX, allows a Magistrate to acquit an accused in a summons case if the complainant is absent.
Section 259, found in Chapter XXI, allows a Magistrate to discharge an accused in certain warrant cases (compoundable or non-cognizable) before a charge is framed if the complainant is absent.
Chapter XVIII, which governs committal inquiries, contains no provision for the acquittal or discharge of an accused due to the complainant's failure to attend court.
application: The Court determined that the analogies to Sections 247 and 259 were invalid because those sections provide for specific situations distinct from a committal inquiry.
Section 247 was deemed inapplicable because the proceeding was a committal inquiry, not a trial of a summons case (an offense punishable with less than one year's imprisonment).
Section 259 was also found inapplicable because the Magistrate was not conducting a trial of a warrant case under Chapter XXI.
The Court then examined the procedure under Chapter XVIII and noted the complete absence of any provision allowing for acquittal or discharge based on the complainant's absence.
The Court interpreted this absence not as an accidental omission but as a "deliberate departure" from the rules governing summons and warrant cases.

The legislative intent, according to the Court, was for the Magistrate to proceed with the committal inquiry regardless of the complainant's absence, as a specific provision would have been included otherwise.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the provisions for acquittal or discharge due to a complainant's absence in summons (Section 247) and warrant (Section 259) cases cannot be applied by analogy to a committal inquiry under Chapter XVIII, as Chapter XVIII deliberately omits any such provision.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the continued presence of the complainant, who is the 'person aggrieved' under Section 198 of the Criminal Procedure Code, is necessary for the continuation of a committal inquiry after cognizance has been taken on their complaint.
appellant_arguments: The requirement under Section 198 for a complaint by an 'aggrieved person' applies not only to the initiation of proceedings but also to their continuation.
If the court cannot take cognizance without a complaint from the aggrieved person, it cannot proceed with the inquiry unless that condition (the presence of the aggrieved person) continues to exist.
Upon the death of the complainant, the complaint must be treated as abated.
respondent_arguments: Section 198 merely creates a bar to taking cognizance, which is removed once a proper complaint is filed by the aggrieved person. After that, the section's purpose is fulfilled ('works itself out').
The Code does not state that the complainant must remain present throughout the proceedings for the court to retain jurisdiction.

The prosecution can be continued by another person, such as the complainant's mother, as permitted under Section 495 of the Code, which allows the court to authorize 'any person' to conduct the prosecution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the provisions for acquittal or discharge of an accused due to the complainant's absence in summons cases (Section 247) and warrant cases (Section 259) can be applied by analogy to a committal inquiry under Chapter XVIII of the Criminal Procedure Code.
appellant_arguments: The principles from the chapters on summons and warrant cases, where the complainant's absence can lead to the acquittal or discharge of the accused, should be applied by analogy to committal inquiries.
respondent_arguments: Chapter XVIII, which governs committal inquiries, is distinct and does not contain any provision for acquitting or discharging the accused due to the complainant's absence.
This lack of a provision is a deliberate legislative choice, not an accidental omission, distinguishing committal inquiries from summons and warrant cases.
The intention of the legislature was for the Magistrate to proceed with the inquiry even if the complainant is absent.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 198 of the Criminal Procedure Code creates a bar to a court taking cognizance of certain offenses, which is removed once a complaint is filed by the proper aggrieved person. After this initial condition is met, the section is fulfilled, and the continued presence of the complainant is not necessary for the court to proceed with the inquiry.
obiter: In committal proceedings instituted otherwise than on a police report, there is no provision for the acquittal or discharge of the accused due to the complainant's failure to attend court, which is a deliberate departure from the procedures for summons and warrant cases.
The Code does not state what consequence follows if the complainant remains absent at any subsequent hearing after filing the complaint in a committal proceeding.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Section 198 of the Criminal Procedure Code creates a bar to taking cognizance that is removed once a complaint is filed by the proper aggrieved person; the section then 'works itself out' and does not require the complainant's continued presence. A committal inquiry under Chapter XVIII does not terminate upon the complainant's death or absence because, unlike the chapters on summons and warrant cases, it contains no provision for the acquittal or discharge of the accused on that ground, a difference the court views as a deliberate legislative choice.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation: The court analyzed the structure of the Criminal Procedure Code, concluding that the absence of a provision for acquittal/discharge in Chapter XVIII, when such provisions exist in other chapters (XX and XXI), is a deliberate legislative choice and not an omission to be filled by analogy.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the condition for initiating proceedings (a complaint by an aggrieved person) must continue throughout was rejected. The court held: 'Once the bar is removed, because the proper person has filed a complaint, the section works itself out. If any other restriction was also there the Code would have said so.'

The attempt to apply provisions from summons cases (Section 247) and warrant cases (Section 259) by analogy was rejected because those sections apply to different types of proceedings (trials) governed by distinct chapters of the Code.

The court found that the lack of a provision in Chapter XVIII for acquitting or discharging an accused due to the complainant's absence 'is not an omission but a deliberate departure from the Chapters on the trial of summons and warrant cases.'
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that Section 198's purpose is fulfilled once a proper complaint is filed, stating, 'Section 198 Cr. P.C. creates a bar which has to be removed belcre cognisance is taken. Once the bar is removed because the proper person has filed a complaint, the section works itself out.'

The court agreed that Chapter XVIII is distinct and its silence on the matter means the inquiry should proceed, reasoning, 'The intention appears to be that the Magistrate should proceed with the inquiry because had it not been so intended, the Code would have said so.'
The court affirmed that another person, like the complainant's mother, could continue the prosecution, stating she 'may continue the prosecution herself or through a pleader' under Section 495.
policy_considerations: The court expressed a reluctance to create a procedural loophole that would halt serious criminal cases, stating: 'We see no reason why we should be astute to find a lacuna in the procedural law by which the trial of such important cases would be stultified by the death of a complainant when all that the s. 198 requires is the removal of the bar.'
